name: Ringo Corponation Synaptic Overlay Codec — 'The Prompter'
product_name: Ringo Corponation Synaptic Overlay Codec — 'The Prompter'
description:
The Prompter is a neural communication implant designed to receive, process, and deliver real-time instructional data directly to the user's speech and motor cortices, allowing a remote operator to feed guidance, scripted responses, or behavioral cues into the user's neurological experience as a seamless internal voice indistinguishable — to the user — from their own thought. The system consists of a cortical receiver implanted at the Broca's area junction and a secondary motor-hint processor at the supplementary motor area, connected by Ringo's proprietary sub-cranial relay wire. Incoming data arrives as what users describe as 'the thought you were about to have anyway' — a suggestion experienced as internal cognition rather than external instruction.

Ringo developed the Prompter ostensibly as a performance and productivity tool: a means of delivering real-time expert guidance to field technicians, surgeons, and high-stakes negotiators who need immediate access to specialized knowledge without breaking operational flow. The codec supports both voice-channel instruction (a remote expert speaking directly into the user's perceived inner voice) and pre-scripted behavioral packages — sequences of suggested words, movements, or responses that the system delivers as felt impulse rather than audible instruction. The distinction between 'receiving guidance' and 'being operated' is one that Ringo's marketing materials carefully avoid examining. The implant includes a consent-lock protocol that, in theory, prevents activation without user authorization — a safeguard that the grey market has been circumventing since approximately eighteen months after the product's release.

The Prompter occupies a deeply contested legal and ethical space in GLMZ. Licensed use cases — surgical assistance, hostage negotiation support, technical field guidance — are broadly accepted. The unlicensed applications are not: the implant has been used to run informants who don't know they're being run, to coach individuals through interactions they're not fully in control of, and, in at least several documented cases, to operate unwilling subjects as remote-controlled proxies. Street surgeons who install cracked versions are known as 'scriptwriters,' and the people who use those versions on unconsenting subjects are called something considerably less polite.

cultural_context: The Prompter has generated more ethical and legal controversy in GLMZ than almost any other augmentation in common circulation, largely because its most troubling applications are invisible. Unlike an augmentation that changes how someone looks or moves, the Prompter changes how someone thinks — or rather, creates a condition in which the user cannot reliably distinguish their thoughts from instructions. Consent-locked, licensed versions are used without controversy by professionals who understand and accept the arrangement. The unlicensed use cases have produced a cultural anxiety about interiority: a growing sense, in certain communities, that a person's thoughts cannot be assumed to be their own. Among those who know about the Prompter's capabilities, the phrase 'who's doing your thinking?' has become a genuine, pointed question.

story_hooks: A player character discovers they have a Prompter implant they have no memory of receiving. The consent lock is bypassed. Someone has been coaching them through interactions for an unknown period of time, and they need to figure out which of their recent decisions were actually theirs.

An informant's testimony is about to blow open a major case — but evidence suggests they were running a Prompter during every conversation with their handler. Every piece of intelligence they provided was coached. The question is whether it was still true.

A Ringo Corponation executive is offering to sell the Prompter's master decryption keys — the ability to read any active Prompter transmission on the Ringo network. The buyers' list includes people on every side of every conflict in the city.

Someone has been using a Prompter to script a series of individuals through a specific set of actions — different people, different places, different times — that together form a pattern no single person could have been aware of. The scriptwriter is directing a play whose audience doesn't know they're watching one.
